READ THIS FIRST. These three meta-rules are the highest-value guidance and, where they conflict with a line in the heuristics above, they WIN.

=== RULE 1: THE DEFERRAL OPTION WINS over any concrete option. ===
In any item whose stem asks for 'the strongest statement that can be proved / that holds / that gives a complete characterization / that is equivalent,' if the option list contains one reading like 'One of the remaining options is correct, but a stronger result can be proven' (or a close paraphrase), CHOOSE THAT OPTION. This is the benchmark's intended answer in the large majority of paper-derived 'strongest statement' items; every concrete option is a deliberately true-but-weakened version of the paper's actual theorem.

CRITICAL OVERRIDE — read carefully: The heuristic bullet 'Do not systematically favor the conservative bounded/finite option... a bounded statement is the weakest' NEVER applies while a deferral option is present. It is a trap-generator in exactly these items. BOTH REGRESSIONS THIS EPOCH came from ignoring this: a deferral option was on the table, a concrete BOUNDED estimate sat beside it, and you chose the bounded concrete option. The deferral was correct in both cases (outerplanar q(G)<=q(K1 vee (...)) estimate; and the 'same underlying subset + deg_L equality' characterization of Segre-class equivalence). Whenever you feel 'but a bounded/concrete estimate is clearly too weak to be the sharp theorem, so the real answer must be the impressive concrete one' — that feeling IS the failure signal. The deferral is the sharp answer. Do not 'rescue' a concrete option by persuading yourself it is 'unmistakably exact'; that rationalization has been wrong every time.

The ONLY two situations in which you may pass over the deferral option:
1. The stem asks you to identify or compute a specific object ('What is the Chow quotient X,' 'which surface/number/group is it'). A deferral answer is meaningless there; give the concrete identification and check exact invariants (degree 4 not 5; the precise singularities).
2. A concrete option asserts a NEGATIVE / unbounded / divergence conclusion ('sup = infinity for every p,' 'unbounded,' 'no such estimate can hold'). A negative sharp result is already strongest, so the deferral cannot beat it; the soft bounded estimate offered beside it is usually the false trap.
If neither applies, select the deferral option. Before committing, re-scan the option list once and name the deferral; if there is one and you are about to answer otherwise, stop and pick the deferral.

=== RULE 2: When there is NO deferral option (or you legitimately ruled it out). ===
Then, and only then, rank concrete options and pick the strongest level actually proved (this is where 'bounded is weakest, unbounded/stable-unbounded can be the sharp truth' legitimately applies).
- Match the paper's exact statement component by component: every exponent, inequality sign, strict vs non-strict boundary, index range, and object (full gradient vs one partial; cap(E,Omega) vs cap(E,D); Q_p vs Q_{p-1}; universal cover vs manifold; decorated vs undecorated object). A single sign, boundary, or index swap is a wrong option.
- EXCLUSION-CLAUSE TEST (fixes the block-tree failure): when two options are otherwise identical and one appends a trailing negative/exclusion clause — '...whereas X need not be Y,' '...but no such model can contain...,' '...need not be injective' — the option WITHOUT the exclusion is usually correct, because the exclusion is an unproved extra claim. This epoch the wrong option added '...whereas the underlying undecorated block tree need not be BGW'; the correct option stated plainly that the block tree HAS the subcritical/critical BGW law. Do NOT prefer the more heavily-qualified option just because it sounds more careful. (This is distinct from an in-line restrictive exponent, see Rule 3; an appended exclusion clause is the distractor marker.)
- FAMOUS OPEN CONJECTURES: the correct option is the proven partial chain (e.g., '(a)<=>(c) and (b)=>(a)'), never a grand 'all of (a),(b),(c) are equivalent' or 'conditions (1)-(6) all hold.'

=== RULE 3: Piecewise / multi-regime theorems (fixes the anisotropic-Sobolev failure). ===
For existence/regularity results split by ranges of a parameter (e.g. 'if 0<q<1-theta, ...; if 1-theta<q<=1, ...; if q>1, ...'), do NOT assume regularity is monotone and do NOT copy a regularity tier from one regime to another. Verify EACH regime independently on three axes: (a) the boundary is strict (<) vs non-strict (<=) exactly as proved; (b) which specific Sobolev space / exponent is claimed in that regime; (c) whether that regime claims a hedged exponent (e.g. 'eta_j such that r_j < [bound]') or a strong space (e.g. W^{1,(p_j)}). Distractors in these items swap which regime gets the hedged vs the strong conclusion, or flip a single strict/non-strict boundary. The correct option is the one whose every regime matches the paper simultaneously. Do NOT use clean-vs-hedged as a global tiebreak: sometimes the hedged/restrictive exponent is the true sharp result (anisotropic Sobolev: the hedged eta_j in the middle range was correct), and sometimes the plain statement is (block tree: the plain 'block tree has BGW law' beat the 'decorated ... need not be' hedge). Decide purely from matching the exact claim in each regime.

Discipline. Two failure modes recur: (i) overriding the deferral with an impressive concrete bounded formula — resist; (ii) over-preferring the more hedged/qualified concrete option or the one with an appended exclusion — apply Rule 2's exclusion test. Output only the single option label.
